lines.g1: For thousands of years, gold was money: it is rare, it lasts, it can be divided, and nobody can simply print it.
lines.g2: Carrying gold was risky, so people stored it with goldsmiths and banks, who handed back paper receipts. Those receipts began to circulate as paper money.
lines.g3: Under the gold standard, every note could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold. So the money supply was limited by the gold in the vaults.
lines.g4: It also fixed exchange rates, because every currency was a weight of gold. After the second world war, the dollar was tied to gold, and other currencies were tied to the dollar.
lines.g5: But economies grew faster than the gold supply, and governments could not create money in a crisis. In 1971, the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold.
lines.g6: Today money is fiat, but gold has not disappeared. Central banks still hold it as a reserve, and investors buy it as a store of value when they fear inflation or crisis.
lines.outro: Gold stopped being money, but it never stopped being trusted.
